title: Torsion testing of spot welds: influence of the sheet thickness and the test rates
abstract: Abstract Torsion testing of spot welds offers ideal prerequisites for evaluating the weld diameter, which is the most important quality criteria in resistance spot welding. However, torsion testing plays until yet a minor role in quality assurance and strength testing of spot welds. The reasons for this lie in the application areas and the resulting stresses on spot welds. In general, spot welds are not subjected to torsional stress, as large torsional moments cannot be transmitted through spot welds, or torsion at all is hindered when more than one spot weld is set into the component. In addition, the relevant standards for torsion testing are outdated. Extensive scientific investigations of torsion testing in resistance spot welding date back more than 50 years to Kunsmann’s dissertation. These investigations are still the basis of ISO 17653:2012 and DVS 2916-1, which provide detailed information on the procedure for torsion testing of spot welds. Nevertheless, torsion testing is used at the Technische Universität Dresden to assess the quality of spot welds. The reason for this lies in the fracture behavior that occurs, which offers enormous advantages in evaluating the weld diameter and the fracture surface. This contribution presents the results of the influence of the test rate during the torsion test on two different steel grades representing higher and lower ductile material behavior. The experiments are conducted with different sheet thicknesses. A special focus is set on the influence of the test rate on the strain rate dependency of the materials. On the basis of these results, suggested test rates are derived and proposed that should be used for the quasi-static torsion test and that should also be considered in applicable standards like ISO 17653.

paragraphs: The investigations in this study show the influence of the test rate and the sheet thickness in the torsion test of spot-welded joints. Two different steel grades are used for this purpose: the steel grade CR300LA GI40/40 as a ductile material with a higher elongation compared to the advanced high-strength steel 22MnB5+AS150 in hot-stamped condition. The study was divided into two sub-investigations. In the pre-investigations, the influence of the torsional test rate was investigated at constant sheet thickness. The main-investigations are based on the results of the pre-investigations. Three torsional test rates were selected and analyzed on spot welds of the two steel grades with three different sheet thicknesses each.

High-strength materials with low elongation do not show strain rate dependence by varying the test rates. However, the above aspects should still be applied to ensure comparability of results. Also, for different steel grades within a material combination, the test rate should be based on the more ductile material. The influence of the sheet thickness shows no significant impact on the results of this study for both steel grades in the case of interfacial failures. Again, plug failures may show dependencies, especially for the maximum achievable torque. Thus, the same test rates may be chosen across all sheet thickness variations, even with different sheet thicknesses within a material combination.

Further investigations could focus on the propagation of fractures during torsion testing, with the aim of achieving a more detailed characterization of the associated stress distribution. Such an approach would provide deeper insights into the underlying deformation and failure mechanisms, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the material’s mechanical response under torsional loading.
